14   Isais, and Lubna Salah’s (“Proposed Intervenors”) motion to intervene and stay.  ECF No. 27.  
15   The Court will deny the motion.                                       
16        On May 19, 2023, Plaintiff City of Hollywood Firefighters’ Pension System filed a 
17   shareholder derivative complaint against Defendant Wells Fargo & Company, as well as certain 
18   directors of Wells Fargo.  ECF No. 1 at 4.  The complaint alleges “breaches of fiduciary duty in 
19   connection with [Wells Fargo’s] failure to comply with federal law, including explicit regulatory 
20   requirements established by federal regulators in multiple consent orders since 2018[.]”  Id.  On 
21   June 20, 2023, Proposed Intervenors filed this motion to intervene and stay.  ECF No. 27.   
22        First, Proposed Intervenors seek to intervene as of right under Federal Rule of Civil 
23   Procedure 24(a).1  The rule is “broadly interpreted in favor of intervention,” and requires a movant

5                                                                         
6   Citizens for Balanced Use v. Mont. Wilderness Ass’n, 647 F.3d 893, 897 (9th Cir. 2011) (citation 
7   omitted).  Courts deciding motions to intervene as of right are “guided primarily by practical 
8   considerations, not technical distinctions.”  Id. (citation and quotations omitted).   
9        In their motion, Proposed Intervenors state that they “have an interest in the transactions 
10   that are the subject of this action, namely, similar and overlapping breaches of fiduciary duty that 
11   harm [Wells Fargo].”  ECF No. 27 at 7.  Plaintiff opposes the motion, contending that “the 
12   derivative nature of Proposed Intervenors’ potential claims precludes them from having a 
13   significant protectable interest.”  ECF No. 33 at 11.                 
14        The Court agrees with Plaintiff that Proposed Intervenors have failed to demonstrate that 
15   they have a significant protectable interest in this litigation.  In “a derivative action, the real party 
16   in interest is the corporation, and the shareholder plaintiff is ‘at best the nominal plaintiff.’”  In re 
17   Facebook, Inc. S’holder Derivative Priv. Litig., 367 F. Supp. 3d 1108, 1130 (N.D. Cal. 2019) 
18   (quoting Ross v. Bernhard, 396 U.S. 531, 538 (1970)).  “Any remedies resulting from the action 
19   belong to the corporation and it is bound by the result of the suit.”  Id. (internal quotations 
20   omitted).  Because of the derivative nature of this action, Proposed Intervenors have no significant 
21   protectable interest in the outcome of this litigation.               
22        Even if Proposed Intervenors could establish a significant protectable interest, they would 
23   still be unable to demonstrate adequacy of representation.  “When an applicant for intervention 
24   and an existing party have the same ultimate objective, a presumption of adequacy of 
25   representation arises.”  Arakaki v. Cayetano, 324 F.3d 1078, 1086 (9th Cir. 2003) (citing League 
26   of United Latin Am. Citizens v. Wilson, 131 F.3d 1297, 1305 (9th Cir. 1997)).  “The prospective 
27                                                                         
1   intervenor bears the burden of demonstrating that existing parties do not adequately represent its 
2   interests.”  United States v. City of Los Angeles, Cal., 288 F.3d 391, 398 (9th Cir. 2002).   
3        Proposed Intervenors contend that Plaintiff does not adequately represent Wells Fargo’s 
4   interests, as Plaintiff “effectively ignored its obligation to conduct a diligent [Delaware General 
5   Corporation Law Section 220] investigation before filing suit[.]”  ECF No. 27 at 9.  Specifically, 
6   Proposed Intervenors argue that they made their § 220 demand in March 2023, and therefore any 
7   proposed claims would be “based on misconduct found by the [2022 Consumer Financial 
8   Protection Bureau Order].”  ECF No. 35 at 4.2  But this is not enough to overcome the 
9   presumption that Plaintiff can adequately represent Wells Fargo’s interests.  Plaintiff conducted a 
10   § 220 investigation, and its complaint likewise “asserts repeated Board failures in the face of red 
11   flags from 2018 through April 2021.”  ECF No. 33 at 13 (emphasis in original).  Indeed, Plaintiff’s 
12   complaint references the 2022 CFPB Order on multiple occasions.  See, e.g., ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 13, 
13   167, 169.  It neither appears that Plaintiff “rushe[d] to file a Caremark claim,” South v. Baker, 62 
14   A.3d 1, 23 (Del. Ch. 2012), nor is it likely that Plaintiff is “in a weaker position” to claim demand 
15   futility.  ECF No. 27 at 9.  To be sure, any derivative complaint that Proposed Intervenors’ may 
16   file would cover a slightly different time period than Plaintiff’s complaint, and their claims are not 
17   likely to be “completely subsumed in Plaintiff’s claims.”  ECF No. 35 at 4.  The Court, however, 
18   is not convinced that this is sufficient to deem Plaintiff an inadequate representative of Wells 
19   Fargo’s interests in this action.                                     
20        “Failure to satisfy any one of the requirements is fatal” to a Rule 24(a) request.  Perry v. 
21   Proposition 8 Off. Proponents, 587 F.3d 947, 950 (9th Cir. 2009).  Proposed Intervenors have not 
22   demonstrated a significantly protectable interest, and they have failed to establish that they are not 
23   adequately represented by Plaintiff.  Accordingly, their motion to intervene as of right is denied.3

    on September 27, 2021,” and “reaches conduct dating back to September 27, 2018.”  ECF No. 33 
27                                                                         
    at 14–15.                                                             
1        In the alternative, Proposed Intervenors seek permissive intervention.  ECF No. 27 at 10. 
2   To obtain the right of permissive intervention, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(b) “requires (1) 
3   an independent ground for jurisdiction; (2) a timely motion; and (3) a common question of law 
4   and fact between the movant’s claim or defense and the main action.”  Freedom from Religion 
5   Found., Inc. v. Geithner, 644 F.3d 836, 843 (9th Cir. 2011) (citations omitted).  Additionally, “the 
6   court must consider whether the intervention will unduly delay or prejudice the adjudication of the 
7   original parties’ rights.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 24(b)(3).                 
8        Neither party disputes that Proposed Intervenors’ motion was timely filed or that a 
9   common question of law or fact exists with the underlying action.  As Plaintiff points out, 
10   however, Proposed Intervenors “have not identified independent grounds for jurisdiction, as is 
11   specifically required under Rule 24(b)(1)(B).”  The Court denies Proposed Intervenors’ motion on 
12   that ground.                                                          
13        The Court is also unpersuaded by their remaining argument that intervention will not 
14   unduly delay this litigation.  See Nw. Forest Res. Council v. Glickman, 82 F.3d 825, 839 (denying 
15   a motion to permissively intervene under Rule 24(b) because the proposed intervenor failed to 
16   “assert [an] independent basis for jurisdiction.”).  Although Proposed Intervenors claim that they 
17   “only need a limited stay to ensure that their claims . . . are properly investigated,” they concede 
18   that they “cannot proposed a definitive time for when the stay would end.”  ECF No. 35 at 4.  As 
19   Plaintiff notes, there is “no estimate of how long it will take [Proposed Intervenors] to receive 
20   whatever books and records they have demanded, review the productions, and prepare and file a 
21   derivative complaint[.]”  ECF No. 33 at 16.  This Court is scheduled shortly to determine the 
22   question of lead plaintiff and lead counsel status.  See, e.g., ECF Nos. 81, 84, 85 (calendaring 
23   hearing on motions to appoint lead plaintiff and lead counsel).  Given these impending deadlines,

    Company, No. 23-cv-2445-JST (N.D. Cal. 2023) (“Hollywood Action”), ECF Nos. 48, 50, 81; 
27                                                                         
    Martin v. Black et al., No. 4:23-cv-03564-JST (N.D. Cal. 2023) (“Local 33 Action”), ECF Nos. 
1   05112-JST (N.D. Cal. 2023) (“FPPA Action”).1  For the reasons set forth below, the Court 
2   consolidates the actions under the Hollywood Action; appoints City of Hollywood Firefighters’ 
3   Pension System as Lead Plaintiff; and appoints Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, LLP as Lead 
4   Counsel.                                                              
5   I.   CONSOLIDATION                                                    
6        A.   Legal Standard                                              
7        “When actions involving a common question of law or fact are pending before the court, it 
8   . . . may order all the actions consolidated.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 42(a).  The “district court has broad 
9   discretion under this rule to consolidate cases pending in the same district.”  Investors Research 
10   Co. v. Dist. Court, 877 F.2d 777, 777 (9th Cir. 1989).  “In determining whether or not to 
11   consolidate cases, the Court should ‘weigh the interest of judicial convenience against the 
12   potential for delay, confusion and prejudice.’”  Zhu v. UCBH Holdings, Inc., 682 F. Supp. 2d 
13   1049, 1052 (N.D. Cal. 2010) (quoting Southwest Marine, Inc. v. Triple A Machine Shop, Inc., 720 
14   F. Supp. 805, 806–807 (N.D. Cal. 1989)).                              
15        B.   Discussion                                                  
16        Each Plaintiff moves to consolidate the respective cases.  See Hollywood Action, ECF No. 
17   48 at 6l; ECF No. 50 at 7; ECF No. 81 at 9.  Each Plaintiff alleges breaches of fiduciary duty 
18   against Wells Fargo’s directors and officers for their failure to oversee the Company’s compliance 
19   with regulatory consent orders, and all Plaintiffs agree that each action therefore involves 
20   numerous common questions of law and fact.  Id.  Given this factual and legal overlap, judicial 
21   convenience and the just resolution of the parties’ claims would be best served through 
22   consolidation.  Therefore, the Court grants the motion to consolidate the Local 33, FPPA, and 
23   Hollywood actions.                                                    
24                                                                         
25                                                                         
26                                                                         
27                                                                         
1   II.  APPOINTMENT OF LEAD PLAINTIFF AND LEAD COUNSEL                   
2        A.   Legal Standard                                              
3        Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23.1, a district court has the inherent authority to 
4   appoint lead counsel and/or lead plaintiff as long as the plaintiff “fairly and adequately 
5   represent[s] the interests of shareholders or members who are similarly situated in enforcing the 
6   right of the corporation or association.”  Berg v. Guthart, 2014 WL 3749780, at *2 (N.D.Cal., 
7   2014) (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 23.1(a)).  For purposes of Rule 23.1, “[a]n adequate representative 
8   must have the capacity to vigorously and conscientiously prosecute a derivative suit and be free 
9   from economic interests that are antagonistic to the interests of the class.”  Larson v. Dumke, 900 
10   F.2d 1363, 1367 (9th Cir. 1990).                                      
11        To assess a proposed plaintiff’s adequacy, courts in this circuit consider the following 
12   factors: (1) indications that the plaintiff is not the true party in interest; (2) the plaintiff's 
13   unfamiliarity with the litigation and unwillingness to learn about the suit; (3) the degree of control 
14   exercised by the attorneys over the litigation; (4) the degree of support received by the plaintiff 
15   from other shareholders; (5) the lack of any personal commitment to the action on the party of the 
16   representative plaintiff; (6) the remedy sought by plaintiff in the derivative action; (7) the relative 
17   magnitude of plaintiff’s personal interests as compared to his interest in the derivative action itself; 
18   and (8) plaintiff's vindictiveness toward the defendants.  Nicolow v. Hewlett Packard Co., 2013 
19   WL 792642, at *7 (N.D. Cal. 2013) (citing Larson, 900 F.2d at 1367)).  Courts have also 
20   considered the factors found in the PSLRA and the Manual for Complex Litigation, “such as the 
21   quality of the plaintiff’s pleadings, the vigorousness of the plaintiff’s efforts, the size of the 
22   plaintiff’s financial interest, and a general preference for institutional investors.”  Id.; accord Berg, 
23   2014 WL 3749780 at *4.                                                
24        B.   Discussion                                                  
25        The Court begins by noting that each proposed lead plaintiff and lead counsel would 
26   adequately represent the interests of shareholders.  The proposed lead plaintiffs as a group are 
27   sophisticated, institutional investors who have experience participating as lead plaintiffs in similar 
1   Congress’ reasoning underlying the PSLRA’s preference for institutional investors in the context 
2   of a derivative action).  Each maintains a large financial interest in Wells Fargo:  Local 33 holds 
3   17,387 shares (0.22% of its total portfolio); FPPA holds 48,821 shares (0.03% of its total 
4   portfolio); and Hollywood holds 11,200 shares (0.17% of its total portfolio).  See Hacker v. 
5   Peterschmidt, 2006 WL 2925683, at *5 (N.D.Cal. 2006) (proposed co-lead plaintiffs who 
6   collectively held 5,500 shares “demonstrated substantial financial interest in the outcome of these 
7   actions”).  Each proposed lead counsel is similarly qualified in that each has significant experience 
8   obtaining favorable results as lead counsel in shareholder derivative litigation.  Therefore, the 
9   Court concludes that each of the competing movants has the capacity to vigorously prosecute this 
10   derivative action.                                                    
11        What distinguishes Hollywood from the other plaintiffs is its longer actionable period.  
12   Hollywood Firefighters served its Section 220 Demand on September 27, 2021, and therefore can 
13   timely assert claims based on conduct dating back to September 27, 2018.  Lebanon Cty. Emps.’ 
14   Ret. Fund v. Collis, 287 A.3d 1160, 1208–09 (Del. Ch. 2022) (“[F]or a derivative action in which 
15   the plaintiff has sought books and records, the court can calculate the actionable [three-year] 
16   period using an earlier date tied to the plaintiff’s diligent pursuit of its informational rights.”).  In 
17   contrast, FPPA issued its books and records demand on March 17, 2023, and can timely assert 
18   claims based only on conduct dating back to March, 17, 2020.  Local 33 did not make a Section 
19   220 demand and can timely assert claims based only on conduct dating back to July 18, 2020, 
20   three years prior to filing its complaint.  Hollywood’s actionable period is thus eighteen months 
21   and twenty-one months longer, respectively, than those of the other Plaintiffs. 
22        Hollywood contends that this extended actionable period is critical because Wells Fargo’s  
23   misconduct between September 2018 and March 2020 period informed the $250 million OCC fine 
24   in September 2021 and the $3.7 billion CFPB Consent Order in December 2022.  Hollywood 
25   alleges that during this period, “Wells Fargo’s improper focus on the Asset Cap and earnings 
26   issues, and the Board’s unwillingness to hold senior management responsible, was reflected in 
27   multiple years’ worth of noncompliance with the various Consent Orders to which Wells Fargo

11                                                                         
               Defendants.                                                

12                                                                         
13        Before the Court is Timothy Himstreet and Montini Family Trust’s (collectively, 
14   “Proposed Intervenors” or “State Plaintiffs”) motion to intervene and stay or dismiss.  ECF No. 
15   127.  The Court will grant the motion and stay the case.              
16   I.   BACKGROUND                                                       
17        This derivative shareholder action arises out of defendant Wells Fargo’s alleged “breaches 
18   of fiduciary duty in connection with their failure to comply with federal law, including explicit 
19   regulatory requirements established by federal regulators in multiple consent orders since 2018[.]”  
20   ECF No. 116 at 4.                                                     
21        On January 2, 2024, City of Hollywood Firefighters’ Pension System (“City of 
22   Hollywood”) was selected as Lead Plaintiff in this action, ECF No. 105, and it filed its 
23   consolidated shareholder derivative complaint on February 16, 2024.  ECF No. 116.  The 
24   consolidated complaint asserts one claim of relief against the Individual Defendants for breach of 
25   fiduciary duty.1                                                      
26                                                                         

27                                                                         
    1 The Individual Defendants in the City of Hollywood action include Steven D. Black, Mark A. 
1        The earlier-filed action is Timothy Himstreet and Montini Family Trust v. Charles W. 
2   Scharf, et al., No. CGC-22-599223 (Cal. Super. Ct. April 19, 2022) (the “State Action”), a 
3   shareholder derivative action brought by Proposed Intervenors against Wells Fargo and its board 
4   of directors and officers, currently pending in San Francisco Superior Court.  It pleads claims for 
5   breach of fiduciary duty, unjust enrichment, and waste of corporate assets.  ECF No. 59-1 at 58–
6   60.  On October 5, 2022, the State Court issued an order overruling Wells Fargo’s demurrer to the 
7   complaint, id. at 68, which was thereafter affirmed by the Court of Appeal of the State of 
8   California, First Appellate District, id. at 81.                      
9        Proposed Intervenors now bring this motion to intervene pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 24, 
10   and to stay or dismiss pursuant to Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 
11   U.S. 800 (1976) (“Colorado River”).                                   
12   II.  DISCUSSION                                                       
13        A.   Mandatory Intervention                                      
14        Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(a)(2) provides for intervention as a matter of right 
15   where the potential intervenor “claims an interest relating to the property or transaction that is the 
16   subject of the action, and is so situated that disposing of the action may as a practical matter 
17   impair or impede the movant’s ability to protect its interest, unless existing parties adequately 
18   represent that interest.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 24(a)(2).                  
19        An applicant for intervention as of right must satisfy four criteria:  “(1) the applicant must 
20   timely move to intervene; (2) the applicant must have a significantly protectable interest relating to 
21   the property or transaction that is the subject of the action; (3) the applicant must be situated such 
22   that the disposition of the action may impair or impede the party’s ability to protect that interest; 
23   and (4) the applicant’s interest must not be adequately represented by existing parties.”  Arakaki v. 
24   Cayetano, 324 F.3d 1078, 1083 (9th Cir. 2003) (citing Donnelly v. Glickman, 159 F.3d 405, 409 
25   (9th Cir. 1998)).  “Failure to satisfy any one of the requirements is fatal to the application, and [the 
26   Court] need not reach the remaining elements if one of the elements is not satisfied.”  Perry v. 
27   Proposition 8 Off. Proponents, 587 F.3d 947, 950 (9th Cir. 2009).     
1             1.   Significantly Protectable Interest                     
2        “The requirement of a significantly protectable interest is generally satisfied when ‘the 
3   interest is protectable under some law, and that there is a relationship between the legally 
4   protected interest and the claims at issue.’”  Araki, 324 F.3d at 1084 (quoting Sierra Club v. EPA, 
5   995 F.2d 1478, 1484 (9th Cir. 1993)).                                 
6        Proposed Intervenors recognize that, “unlike in a typical motion to intervene,” they “are 
7   not third parties seeking to participate in the Federal Action.”  ECF No. 127 at 15.  Rather, they 
8   contend that “[a]s a result of satisfying . . . demand futility requirements, [they] are now 
9   authorized to act on Wells Fargo’s behalf and to pursue the Company’s claims.”  Id.  City of 
10   Hollywood responds that “[t]he State Court’s order holding that demand was excused did nothing 
11   more than establish State Plaintiffs’ ‘standing to sue’ derivatively on behalf of Wells Fargo for the 
12   specific claims as to which demand was excused.”  ECF No. 134 at 12 (citing Advanced Advisors 
13   G. P. v. Berman, No. LACV1401420JAKSSX, 2014 WL 12772264, at *6 (C.D. Cal. Sept. 16, 
14   2014)).                                                               
15        “When conducting a demand futility analysis, a Delaware court proceeds on a claim-by-
16   claim and director-by-director basis.”  Ontario Provincial Council of Carpenters’ Pension Tr. 
17   Fund v. Walton, No. 2021-0827-JTL, 2023 WL 3093500, at *29 (Del. Ch. Apr. 26, 2023); see 
18   Beam v. Stewart, 833 A.2d 961, 977 n.48 (Del. Ch. 2003) (“Demand futility analysis is conducted 
19   on a claim-by-claim basis”), aff’d, 845 A.2d 1040 (Del. 2004).  If demand is excused as futile, it is 
20   solely “for the purposes of that claim.”  Ontario Provincial Council of Carpenters’ Pension Tr. 
21   Fund, 2023 WL 3093500, at *29.  Thus, “[i]f another set of claims arises out of a different nucleus 
22   of operative facts or concerns a different transaction, then the court moves on to the next claim and 
23   repeats the process.”  Id.                                            
24        Although Proposed Intervenors have standing to sue derivatively on behalf of Wells Fargo 
25   for specific claims, they cite no authority (and the Court is aware of none) that grants them a 
26   significantly protectable interest in order to seek a stay or dismissal of the federal action on “their 
27   behalf, in connection with their entitlement to pursue litigation for Wells Fargo[.]”  ECF No. 137 
1        “Failure to satisfy any one of the requirements is fatal” to a Rule 24(a) request.  Perry, 587 
2   F.3d at 950.  Because Proposed Intervenors have not demonstrated a significant protectable 
3   interest, their motion to intervene as of right is denied.  The Court declines to reach the remaining 
4   factors.                                                              
5        B.   Permissive Intervention                                     
6        Turning to permissive intervention, “[d]istrict courts have discretion to permit an entity to 
7   intervene if the entity raises a claim that has a legal or factual issue or issues in common with the 
8   underlying action.  In exercising their discretion, courts must consider whether intervention will 
9   unduly delay or prejudice the existing parties.”  In re Benny, 791 F.2d 712, 722 (9th Cir. 1986) 
10   (citing Fed. R. Civ. P. 24(b)(1)(B)) (“On timely motion, the court may permit anyone to intervene 
11   who . . . has a claim or defense that shares with the main action a common question of law or 
12   fact.”).                                                              
13        City of Hollywood concedes that Proposed Intervenors’ claims “share common questions 
14   of law and fact with [their] claims.”  ECF No. 134 at 13.  Therefore, permissive intervention in 
15   this case turns on whether intervention will unduly delay or prejudice the existing parties.  
16   Proposed Intervenors contend that their motion “is brought at an early stage in the federal 
17   proceedings and without any undue delay.”  ECF No. 127 at 20.  The Court agrees that the federal 
18   action is still in early stages—notably, the Court has yet to decide the question of demand futility.  
19   As a result, Proposed Intervenors have demonstrated that they are entitled to permissively 
20   intervene in this action.                                             
21        C.   Colorado River Stay or Dismissal                            
22        Having concluded that Proposed Intervenors are entitled to permissively intervene, the 
23   Court now addresses Proposed Intervenors’ Colorado River motion.      
24        “Generally, as between state and federal courts, the rule is that ‘the pendency of an action 
25   in the state court is no bar to proceedings concerning the same matter in the Federal court having 
26   jurisdiction.’”  Colorado River, 424 U.S. at 817 (quoting McClellan v. Carland, 217 U.S. 268, 282 
27   (1910)).  In rare cases, “there are principles unrelated to considerations of proper constitutional 
1   contemporaneous exercise of concurrent jurisdictions, either by federal courts or by state and 
2   federal courts.”  Colorado River, 424 U.S. at 817.  In the interest of “[w]ise judicial 
3   administration, giving regard to conservation of judicial resources and comprehensive disposition 
4   of litigation,” a district court can dismiss or stay a federal suit “due to the presence of a concurrent 
5   state proceeding”  Id. at 817–18.                                     
6        “No matter how the Colorado River doctrine is formally characterized, however, one 
7   principle is clear:  a stay of federal litigation in favor of state court proceedings ‘is the exception, 
8   not the rule.’”  Ernest Bock, LLC v. Steelman, 76 F.4th 827, 835 (9th Cir. 2023), cert. denied, 144 
9   S. Ct. 554 (2024) (quoting Colorado River, 424 U.S. at 813).  “Only the clearest of justifications 
10   will warrant” dismissal or a stay.  Colorado River, 424 U.S. at 813.      
11        The Ninth Circuit has articulated eight factors to determine whether a Colorado River stay 
12   is justified:  “(1) which court first assumed jurisdiction over any property at stake; (2) the 
13   inconvenience of the federal forum; (3) the desire to avoid piecemeal litigation; (4) the order in 
14   which the forums obtained jurisdiction; (5) whether federal law or state law provides the rule of 
15   decision on the merits; (6) whether the state court proceedings can adequately protect the rights of 
16   the federal litigants; (7) the desire to avoid forum shopping; and (8) whether the state court 
17   proceedings will resolve all issues before the federal court.”  R.R. St. & Co. Inc. v. Transp. Ins. 
18   Co., 656 F.3d 966, 978–79 (9th Cir. 2011).  The factors need not be evaluated like a “mechanical 
19   checklist,” but rather should be applied “in a pragmatic, flexible manner with a view to the 
20   realities of the case at hand.”  Moses H. Cone Mem’l Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1, 
21   21 (1983).  “The weight to be given to any one factor may vary greatly from case to case.”  Id. at 
22   16.2                                                                  
23             1.   Resolution of All Issues in State Court Proceedings    
24        Because “[p]arallelism is necessary but not sufficient to counsel in favor of abstention,” the 
25   Court addresses the final factor first.  Seneca Ins. Co., Inc. v. Strange Land, Inc., 862 F.3d 835, 
26
